lessons.title: Centers and wingers
lessons.objective: Explain what centers and wingers do.

payload.prompt: Match the forward position to what they do.

pairs.definition: Lines up in the middle, takes faceoffs, handles the puck most, and must defend as well as score.
Plays the left side, supports the center, and covers the left boards in the defensive zone.
Plays the right side, mirrors the left winger, and covers the right boards in the defensive zone.

distractorDefinitions: Skates from the blue line to the goal line on the power play.
Stands in the crease and screens the goalie.

explanation.summary: The center links the line, taking draws and covering the middle of the ice; the wingers work the sides. Everyone on the line defends too.
explanation.sayThisLine: He's the center, so he takes the draw.

payload.prompt: Which player is the center?

image.alt: Three forwards lined up in the offensive zone: one in the middle with the puck, two on the sides.

options.text: The player in the middle with the puck
options.explanation: Correct. The center lines up between the two wingers and usually has the puck first.

options.text: The player on the left side
options.explanation: That is the left winger. Wingers play on the sides of the line.

options.text: The player on the right side
options.explanation: That is the right winger. The center is in the middle.

explanation.correct: Right. The center is in the middle and orchestrates the line's play.
explanation.incorrect: The center lines up between the two wingers. Look for the player in the middle of the formation.
explanation.sayThisLine: Center in the middle, wings on the sides.

cues: Center often controls the puck first

payload.prompt: Why do good centers take almost every faceoff?

options.text: They get a bonus point for each draw they win.
They are skilled at battling for the puck and setting up the play that follows.
options.explanation: Correct. Centers control the puck first on the faceoff, then move it to the wings.

options.text: Only centers are allowed to take faceoffs.

explanation.correct: Right. The faceoff puts the puck in play, and a good center can win it and start the offense.
explanation.incorrect: Centers usually take the draws because winning the puck cleanly lets their line start with possession. Wingers can take a draw when a center is thrown out, but it's the center's specialty.
explanation.sayThisLine: Winning the draw is half the battle.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence about what wingers do.
payload.template: A winger plays on the {{position}} and is responsible for {{duty}} in the offensive zone and {{defense}} in their own end.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Wingers are offensive finishers and defensive anchors on their side of the ice.
explanation.incorrect: Wingers play the boards, finish chances offensively, and cover their side defensively. That is the two-way role.
explanation.sayThisLine: Wingers own the boards and finish plays.

payload.prompt: A two-way center is one who scores lots of goals. True or false?

scene.alt: A center skating hard back toward his own net after a turnover to break up the play.

explanation.correct: False. A two-way center is skilled at both offense AND defense. They forecheck, backcheck, and are responsible defensively.
explanation.incorrect: Two-way means excellent at both scoring and defending. It is about complete play, not just goals.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two-way means they play both ends well.

lessons.title: The defensemen
lessons.objective: Explain what defensemen do and why they shoot from the point.

payload.prompt: Match the defensive concept to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A defender who focuses on stopping the opponent's best players; offensive production is secondary.
A defender who joins the rush, moves the puck, and has high offensive output; some risk defensively.
Two defensemen who play together as a unit, usually paired so one covers defense while the other moves up ice.

explanation.summary: Defensemen have different roles. Some are pure defenders, others add offense. A good pair balances both sides.
explanation.sayThisLine: A balanced pair has a defender and a playmaker.

payload.prompt: Tap where a defenseman shoots from on the power play.

diagram.alt: Overhead view of the offensive zone with the blue line at the top and the net at the bottom.

explanation.correct: Right. The point is just inside the offensive blue line, where defensemen shoot from. Forwards screen the goalie or tip the puck.
explanation.incorrect: Defensemen shoot from the point, just inside the blue line. It's a long shot, so forwards in front screen the goalie or tip it.
explanation.sayThisLine: Point shot: defense with a view, forwards with a screen or tip.

payload.prompt: What is a defenseman's first job when their team gets the puck in their defensive zone?

options.text: Shoot it down the ice immediately.
Move the puck out of the zone, usually by passing to a teammate.
options.explanation: Correct. Breaking the puck out starts the offense and prevents scoring chances.

options.text: Charge at the opponent to force a turnover.

explanation.correct: Right. Defensemen are the primary puck movers exiting their zone. A clean breakout starts good offensive flow.
explanation.incorrect: Defensemen must break the puck out cleanly. They pass to forwards or reverse it to their partner, setting up the rush.
explanation.sayThisLine: Puck out of the zone is the first step to scoring.

payload.prompt: Order how a defense pair handles a rush.

items.text: The other team's forwards carry the puck in with speed.
items.why: The rush starts when the opponent brings the puck up ice.

items.text: One defenseman closes on the puck carrier; the other covers the open man.
items.why: A pair splits the job so the carrier has to pass or shoot from a bad spot.

items.text: They win the puck or force a low-danger shot the goalie can handle.
items.why: Good gap control turns a rush into a shot the goalie can handle.

items.text: They pass it up to a forward to start the breakout.
items.why: Stopping the rush is only half the job; the next pass starts the other team's problem.

explanation.correct: That's the flow. The pair splits the threats, wins or neutralizes the rush, then moves the puck the other way.
explanation.incorrect: Think in steps: the rush comes, the pair splits the job, they neutralize it, and then they start the breakout.
explanation.sayThisLine: The pair stopped the rush and started the breakout.

payload.prompt: What does 'tight gap control' mean for a defenseman?

options.text: Staying close to the puck carrier to force them to pass or shoot quickly.
options.explanation: Correct. Tight gap stops the skater's momentum and options.

options.text: Playing far back to protect the goal.
Switching sides with the other defenseman.

explanation.correct: Right. Tight gap control is an aggressive, smart defense tactic. It takes away time and space.
explanation.incorrect: Gap control is the distance a defenseman keeps from the puck carrier. Tight gap shuts down the rush early.
explanation.sayThisLine: Tight gap stops the rush before it starts.

lessons.title: The goalie
lessons.objective: Explain the goalie's job and gear.

payload.prompt: Which player is the goalie?

image.alt: Two players: one in regular skates and jersey, one in large pads, mask, glove and blocker.

options.text: The player with the large pads and mask
options.explanation: Correct. Goalie gear is distinct and protective.

options.text: The player in regular skates and jersey
options.explanation: That is a skater. The goalie wears much more protective equipment.

explanation.correct: Right. A goalie's gear is immediately recognizable: huge pads, a mask, a blocker and glove, neck protection.
explanation.incorrect: The goalie is the one in the distinctive protective gear. Skaters wear regular jersey and pants with shin pads.
explanation.sayThisLine: You can spot a goalie by the pads and the mask.

cues: Goalie wears a protective mask and helmet
Goalie uses a blocker and trapper glove

payload.prompt: What can a goalie do that other players cannot?

options.text: Wear a helmet with a cage.
Cover the puck with a glove to stop play.
options.explanation: Correct. A goalie can smother the puck; a skater who does that takes a penalty.

options.text: Take the faceoff after a save.

explanation.correct: Right. Freezing the puck is a goalie's special power. A goalie can smother it to stop play, while a skater who closes his hand on it gets a penalty.
explanation.incorrect: Gear and skating aren't rules. The real difference is that a goalie can legally cover the puck with a glove to stop play; a skater who does it is penalized.
explanation.sayThisLine: He froze it to get a faceoff.

payload.prompt: Match the goalie term to what it means.

pairs.definition: Drops to the knees with pads spread wide to block the bottom of the net.
Steering or smothering the puck after a save so the other team has no easy second shot.
Positioning between the puck and net to cut down the shooter's view and scoring area.

explanation.summary: Goalies use stance, positioning, and puck management to stop shots. These are core goaltending skills.
explanation.sayThisLine: He's so square to the puck on those angles.

payload.prompt: Describe a goalie's job.
payload.template: A goalie guards the net from the {{area}}, blocks shots with {{technique}}, and can {{action}} the puck to stop play.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The crease is the goalie's home, pads and positioning do most of the work, and freezing the puck stops play for a breather.
explanation.incorrect: A goalie works in and around the crease, uses pads and positioning to make saves, and can freeze the puck to stop play.
explanation.sayThisLine: Great positioning from him in the crease.

payload.prompt: If a goalie freezes the puck, the other team gets a power play. True or false?

scene.alt: A goalie covering the puck with his glove, with play stopped.

explanation.correct: False. Freezing the puck is legal and often smart. It stops play, brings a faceoff and gives the defense a breather.
explanation.incorrect: Freezing the puck is part of goaltending, not a penalty. Play stops and a faceoff follows; nobody goes to the box.
explanation.sayThisLine: A frozen puck means a faceoff, not a penalty.

lessons.title: Lines and pairs
lessons.objective: Describe the four forward lines and three D pairs.

payload.prompt: Order how a team builds its lineup from best to role.

items.text: First line: the best scorers and playmakers, playing the most minutes.
items.why: The top line usually gets the most ice time and drives the offense.

items.text: Second line: more strong scorers, right behind the first.
items.why: A second scoring line means the other team can't just shut down the top line.

items.text: Third line: often a checking or two-way group, with some secondary scoring.
items.why: It takes tough minutes and relieves the top two lines.

items.text: Fourth line: the fewest minutes, bringing energy and physical play.
items.why: Short, hard shifts keep the lineup fresh and give the top lines a rest.

explanation.correct: That's the usual pecking order: top scorers first, more scoring second, checking and depth third, energy fourth. Coaches shuffle it all the time, but the roles are a good map.
explanation.incorrect: The usual order is top scorers first, more scoring second, checking and depth third, energy and physical play fourth. Coaches adjust it depending on matchups.
explanation.sayThisLine: The first line scores, the fourth line brings the energy.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence about team roster size.
payload.template: A team dresses {{forwards}} forwards in {{flines}} lines and {{defense}} defensemen.

explanation.correct: Right. A full NHL roster: 12 forwards in 4 lines, 6 defensemen in 3 pairs, plus 2 goalies.
explanation.incorrect: An NHL team dresses 12 forwards (4 lines of 3) and 6 defensemen (3 pairs of 2).

payload.prompt: Why is a strong third line important for a team's success?

options.text: The third line scores the most goals.
It adds depth scoring and tough minutes, so the top lines don't have to carry everything.
options.explanation: Correct. Depth lets a team spread the workload and win games when the stars are quiet.

options.text: The third line gets more ice time than the second line.

explanation.correct: Right. Depth keeps the stars from carrying every minute and gives coaches matchup options, including the ability to win when the top line is quiet.
explanation.incorrect: The third line doesn't usually score the most or play more than the second line. Its value is depth: secondary scoring, tough minutes and a rest for the stars.
explanation.sayThisLine: A strong third line is a sign of a well-built team.

payload.prompt: Match the term to what it means about line use.

pairs.definition: The best scorers and playmakers, who usually play the most minutes.
All four lines can score or defend, so the other team can't target one.
A line whose job is shutting down the other team's best players, not scoring.

explanation.summary: Good teams give each line a clear job: score, balance the lineup, or check. That's why fans talk about lines by their role.
explanation.sayThisLine: Their checking line shut down the top line.

payload.prompt: Why do coaches usually keep defense pairs together?

options.text: Chemistry and communication: partners learn where each other will be.
options.explanation: Correct. A familiar pair plays with trust and covers space as a unit.

options.text: The rulebook requires the same two defensemen to stay together.
Paired defensemen take more shots than other defensemen.

explanation.correct: Right. Good pairs anticipate each other, cover for each other and know who jumps up and who stays back. Coaches still break pairs up when it isn't working.
explanation.incorrect: It's a coaching choice, not a rule. Pairs stay together because familiarity helps communication and trust.
explanation.sayThisLine: A good pairing is built on chemistry.

lessons.title: Captains, alternates and scratches
lessons.objective: Understand C, A and healthy scratches.

payload.prompt: What does the captain do?

options.text: Scores the most goals on the team.
Speaks to officials on behalf of the team and is a leader in the locker room.
options.explanation: Correct. The captain is the team's voice and leader.

options.text: Decides which line plays next.

explanation.correct: Right. The captain wears the C and is the player who can talk to the referees on the team's behalf, along with the alternates.
explanation.incorrect: The captain is the team leader and the voice to the officials. It's an honor that reflects leadership, not just scoring.
explanation.sayThisLine: The C means leadership and representation, not the most points.

statement.speaker: Sarah
statement.text: He has an A, so I guess he is kind of the second captain?

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: Alternates (A)
options.explanation: Correct. The A stands for alternate captain.

options.text: Assists (A)
options.explanation: That is a stat. She is talking about the letter on his jersey.

options.text: Attendance (A)
options.explanation: That is not a hockey term. The A is the alternate captain letter.

payload.translation: Alternate captains wear an A and help the captain lead the team. A team has one captain and up to two alternates, and the letters go on the ice with them.

followUps.line: Who else wears a letter on your team?
followUps.why: Shows you know a team has a captain plus alternates.

followUps.line: Does he talk to the refs when the captain is on the bench?
followUps.why: Shows you know the A exists so someone with a letter is always on the ice.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you don't know what the letters mean, asking is smarter than guessing.

payload.prompt: What is a healthy scratch?

options.text: A player who is injured and cannot play.
A player who is healthy but not in the lineup that night by coach's choice.
options.explanation: Correct. The coach may scratch a healthy player for depth, matchups, or performance.

options.text: A player who has been suspended by the league.

explanation.correct: Right. A healthy scratch is a roster decision, not an injury. The coach is sending a message or managing depth.
explanation.incorrect: A healthy scratch is a player the team chose not to play, even though they are not injured. It happens for many reasons.
explanation.sayThisLine: Healthy scratch means they are healthy, just not playing today.

payload.prompt: Complete the description of team leadership.
payload.template: The {{first}} wears the C. The {{second}} wear the A. Both are {{role}} for the team.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The C and A give a team leadership and representation.
explanation.incorrect: The C (captain) and A (alternates) are the team's official leaders and voice to officials.

statement.speaker: Marcus
statement.text: I can't believe they made our best player a healthy scratch tonight. What's the message?

payload.question: What is he really asking?

options.text: Why would the coach sit a healthy star?
options.explanation: Correct. He is questioning the coach's decision.

options.text: Is the player injured?
options.explanation: A healthy scratch means the player is healthy, which is exactly why it's surprising.

options.text: Who is the backup goalie tonight?
options.explanation: That isn't what he's asking. He's wondering about the coach's reason.

payload.translation: A healthy scratch of a top player is unusual. It could mean a matchup choice, a message about effort, or a roster move. The fan wants to know which.

followUps.why: It keeps the chat on what's known rather than guessing.

followUps.line: Do you think he's back in the lineup tomorrow?
followUps.why: Shows you know a healthy scratch is usually a one-game decision.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Not knowing why a player is scratched is fine; asking is better than pretending you understand the team.

payload.prompt: Match the player type to their role.

pairs.definition: A player with an elite shot; finishes scoring chances and plays on top lines.
A hard-working, physical player who wins puck battles in the corners; scoring isn't the main job.
Traditionally, a player who fought and intimidated to protect teammates; much rarer today.
A skilled passer who sets up scoring chances for teammates rather than scoring themselves.

explanation.summary: Hockey talk is full of player types: scorers, passers, hard workers and the old-school enforcer. Each one tells you what a player does for his team.
explanation.sayThisLine: He's a true sniper, that release is unreal.

payload.prompt: Why is calling someone a grinder actually a compliment?

options.text: It means they score a lot of goals.
It means they work hard, play physical, and win battles, even if they do not score much.
options.explanation: Correct. Grinders are valued for their work ethic and defensive play.

options.text: It means they are the team captain.

explanation.correct: Right. Grinders are role players who do the dirty work. That is respect, not an insult.
explanation.incorrect: A grinder gets value from effort and defense, not goals. It is a respected role.
explanation.sayThisLine: Grinders win games in the corners.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: We need more snipers up top and a grinder on the third line.

payload.question: What does the coach want?

options.text: A goal scorer and a hardworking player
options.explanation: Correct. Sniper = scorer, grinder = worker.

options.text: A backup goalie and a new trainer
options.explanation: Sniper and grinder are player-style words, not staff or goalie jobs.

options.text: A new defenseman and a new winger
options.explanation: Sniper and grinder describe playing style, not position.

payload.translation: The coach is saying the team needs a top-line scorer and a hard-working third-line player who wins puck battles.

followUps.line: Who's the sniper on your team?
followUps.why: A friendly question that invites them to tell you about their favorite scorer.

followUps.line: Is that the kind of grinder who also kills penalties?
followUps.why: Shows you know grinders often do the unglamorous special-teams jobs.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If hockey slang sounds unfamiliar, that is normal. Ask what it means rather than guessing.

payload.prompt: Match the hockey personality to what they bring.

pairs.definition: Valuable bench contributor who plays secondary lines and provides stability when top players rest.
A player who can play multiple positions or lines, adding flexibility to the roster.
A steady defenseman trusted with big minutes against the other team's best players.

explanation.summary: Stars get the headlines, but depth players, utility forwards and steady defensemen fill out a roster. Fans use these labels all the time.
explanation.sayThisLine: That depth is why they keep winning.

payload.prompt: Enforcer roles have become less common in modern hockey. True or false?

scene.alt: A player playing skilled defense and forechecking, not relying on physicality.

explanation.correct: True. Modern hockey values skating and skill, and designated fighters have all but disappeared from NHL lineups.
explanation.incorrect: Teams now prefer players who can skate and play both ends over a designated enforcer. The enforcer role has largely faded.
explanation.sayThisLine: That kind of enforcer is hard to find today.
